Intro

You wrote a very interesting blog post, which I'm going to quote, tests are means to an end. The means are unimportant.

Host: There is absolutely amazing stuff that you can do with that testing, but in the end, you are still doing something at the late stages in the game. It's true that everybody in the end in some way, whether they admit it or not, is testing in prod. None of the tools that we have are good enough to guarantee whatever it is.

Sean Allen: Technical debt only hurts if you have to pay it back.

Host: Yes, you can very much get yourself into a position where unfortunately, before you've even found product market fit, you might have debted yourself into a corner. But the idea that exists in a lot of stuff where it's like, oh no, every single bit of debt is bad, it always has to be paid off, it's not born out in reality.

Sean Allen: Sean, great to have you.

Host: Thank you.

Host: We need to start with this crazy fact that we discovered. The first company I ever worked for that did professional software, it was called Sensnet, s e n s e n e t. What was the first company that you worked for?

Host: And they're different companies. Yours was in New York.

Host: Mine was in Budapest, Hungary.

Sean’s path into tech

Host: Yeah. And rewinding the clock a lot before your first job, how did you get into tech? In fact, did you even want to get into tech or was it was music more your thing?

Sean Allen: Music was definitely more my thing, but I graduated from college and I realized I had no idea what I was going to do and I just started going through my address book and the first person I found who said I could come stay with them lived in New York City. So I went and a good friend of mine was also living there and he eventually he was like I couldn't I couldn't find a job. I got close to getting one which was as a speech writer for a US senator, but I did not get that. And a friend got me a job fixing computers at Scholastic. And then another friend told me, hey, if you learn Perl, you can move Boston and you can, you know, there was a bunch of people I'd gone to college with who started a startup. So I learned Pearl and right about the time that I finished being good enough learning Pearl over the course of three to four months to, you know, do that.

Uh, that startup had collapsed and then it started just to be like, uh

Host: It was It was a dot com bust, right? Around that time.

Sean Allen: Well, I I like this. I enjoy it. I'd done it a bit like earlier on when I was like a teenager because I there was a video game, Load Runner, and I I loved Load Runner and I really wanted to to create things that were like Load Runner. So I asked my grandmother to get me a book about computer programming, but I didn't know anything about computer programming and my grandmother didn't know anything about computer programming. So she went to a computer store in uh Fort Worth, Texas, and the guy gave her a book which was uh machine language for the Commodore 64. So I was like, wow, programming is really hard. But yet that's I kind of got started that way and it was the first time I was like, oh, there's a thing that people will pay me lots of money for. And I was like, I have no other thing that people would pay me lots of money for.

I should get really good at this.

Host: And then so how did you get really good at at programming? Like you you then worked at different companies, right?

Sean Allen: I spent an awful lot of my free time um just trying to get better at it. I think I I leaps and bounds I got interested in BOS uh in the 90s. Yes. I was really into BOS and um there were some very interesting and helpful people in that community. There was a guy all the compiler tools for BOS were made by this company called Metroworks that also made compilers for Mac OS at that time. And for some reason the guy who was the head of their uh their compiler group took an interest on the mailing list in helping me learn C++. And there was a there was somebody who was uh new C++ and was really nice on the mailing list as well who um I know I know basically nothing about sci-fi at all. So it didn't mean anything to me that that person turned out to be Neal Stephenson who yes who um who

Host: famous sci-fi author

Sean Allen: yes who basically was just like would exchange like emails with me and advice on on learning like C++ programming which was really early on for me and I mean there were other people as well but those were two who really like stood out to me. Like I've still never read a Neal Stephenson thing. I think I read a couple pages of Snow Crash but it's it's always a fun story to tell people.

Joining Antithesis

Host: Yeah and how did you end up at Antithesis?

Sean Allen: Well the the short version would be is that Will Wilson the CEO sent me a message while I was looking for a new job in December which was just a link to a thing that they'd posted on the who's hiring for uh on Hacker News and said would you be interested in this? It was basically like do you want to do Jepson style things? And my response was that sounds like it could be fun.

Host: And what do you do at Antithesis now?

Sean Allen: I'm on a team called the Red Team and I think if you asked everybody at the company what the Red Team does you'd get probably different answers from almost everyone. Um I would I would put it as Will collected a bunch of really smart people together and was like I want you to use our product the way that customers would use our product. One of the things I've done as part of that is I've intentionally never used the tools which are available to us internally to work with the the product and just done it so that I can only work with it with the exact same tools that uh that customers would have for themselves.

Host: It's kind of a neat concept having an internal team who is a customer team except you know you can talk to them, they will reason with you, they'll they'll explain how the customer thinks.

Sean Allen: Yeah and so we're we all have a lot of experience and we've been given a lot of free rein to do anything as long as it as long as people were looking at it going, oh, that's valuable to the company. So, I worked a lot on on skills for helping agents work better with antithesis. But I mean, I think the stuff that I liked the most um is just doing stuff to teach customers and teach people internally as well. A lot of the stuff that I've learned over the years for how to how to be sure that your software works well um and that, you know, for me that starts way down the stack way before anything that anybody calls testing or whatnot. Yeah, and just talking to people about that. I love meeting people. I love talking to people and it's a subject that I that I really love. I don't know. It's kind of a dream job.

OCaml and type systems

Host: And speaking of dream job, one thing that you've been really going deep into is just different languages which I would call a little bit of exotic languages, not I'm not talking with the mainstream TypeScript or maybe Rust or Go etc. But a few other languages. Can we talk about OCaml specifically? What is OCaml and why are all the hedge funds and finance companies in love with it?

Sean Allen: So, OCaml is a language that came from an academic background primarily uh in France originally. Um and it was it came out at the time when people were trying to combine functional programming with object-oriented stuff. This was a really big deal that people like tried to do particularly in the 90s. At that point it was bolting objects onto everything. Objects were very much seen as the future etc. And it's interesting because the version of OCaml that's actually caught on at places like Jane Street and in other places where it could be used a lot is one where none of the O features in OCaml really get used.

Host: What is the O?

Sean Allen: The O is the object part.

Host: Oh.

Sean Allen: And and there is there is a whole series of features which are very object-oriented about it, but I can't think of anyone I know who does OCaml who actually really uses any of the object-oriented features. But it's it's a language um which is descended from ML, which is a entirely different language of families from like Algol languages where where like Python and Perl and for the most part Ruby, C, C++, these are these are all Algol languages. And then there's a in the ML family of which uh OCaml is is one. There are there are a number of others in there. Uh depending on who you ask, some people will say Haskell's kind of in there, kind of not. And um all the ML languages generally provide a a different set of uh a functionality and capabilities to people. The most famous, I think at this point, ML uh influenced language would be Rust.

There's an awful lot of ML type stuff in Rust. The the sum types, the pattern matching, etcetera, all of this is stuff that came from

Host: ML ML this sounds like a bit like more of a declarative language or what what what is the ML how would you describe it?

Sean Allen: The ML languages are generally uh they're built around strong type systems, right? In the same way that that Rust is built around a a strong type system where you take sum types, which is basically saying it could be one of these three things. They they they're kind of like enumerations uh from something like Java that that people might be familiar with or hey Rust is a lot more popular now, so some people might be familiar with it from there. And you can combine that together with uh pattern matching. And And if you can then also combine that together with exhaustive matching um where what it means is that I have this sum type, which could be say five different things, right? And the way that I the way that I will work on it is instead of an if statement, I do pattern matching, but I'm matching on the type that the thing is.

[clears throat] Um and then you can combine that with exhaustive matching. What you can end up with is a code base where you can make one change and say actually now I have six different things of this instead of five. And the compiler will tell you every single place in your code base where you're not handling that six type. And it it is a gloriously wonderful uh experience.

Host: It it it sounds like the compiler gives you additional testing that you might not get from a compiler in let's say a language like C sharp or or TypeScript what not. The compiler there will tell you the types, but if I understand correctly, the exhaustive matching is the key here and the fact that there is matching, it goes and checks kind of maybe conditions or or assumptions that are in these languages like TypeScript. I'll just use it as an example. It's kind of you know you'll figure it out runtime if something breaks. And here in compile time, there's a lot of structural rules and there's of course like logic. It it goes through there. So you kind of front load a lot of that validation if you will.

Sean Allen: Yeah, all all all of the languages which are ML like in some type of way or are in that general family are very much languages where it's like I want to put as much as possible into static checking in the compiler and have the compiler do work for me.

Host: Okay, so now I understand why some people say who are into Rust that Rust helps you ship fewer bugs because it's an ML it's type language which the compiler will do a lot more work and it will have a lot you know stricter rules that you need to become familiar with, but then in return the compiler just like it erases you a lot of things and it'll give you a compiler error.

Sean Allen: Yeah, early on when I was learning to program, um I was really into like different programming languages and just learning like different things that were possible. And uh fairly early on, I decided I was going to pick one thing and I was going to dedicate myself to that for a while. And uh the two languages I ended up settling on were uh C and Ada. And it was mostly it was C the the choice of C came because I was doing a lot of programming for I think it was Mac OS it was either six or seven. I think it was six at that point. And Apple was converting an awful lot of their stuff from Pascal to C at that time. So I was like, oh, okay, well C could be one that could be interesting. And then Ada was just entirely different

Ada and compiler guarantees

and

Host: What what what is Ada like for those of us like myself who don't know?

Sean Allen: Ada is much more in that very very strict static checking thing. [clears throat] Ada is a language that in a lot of ways was driven by the needs and desires of like what the defense department wanted to have for for knowing that there were not going to be bugs of a language which is very deeply specified and will not let you write incorrect programs.

Host: Yeah, we're talking like literal mission critical stuff.

Sean Allen: Yes, yes, mission critical stuff. NASA, the defense department, etc. These these are types of people who Ada was was aimed at. Ada still exists. It has a small but robust market for people. And the number one thing that the Ada companies really go after is, oh, so you like Rust? How would you like to have some more guarantees? Like that's that's that's where that's where the Ada stuff is. And this is this is one of my great regrets was that I didn't really know much about programming and I didn't really know much about programming languages and I could not get programs to compile in Ada.

Host: In Ada because it's so damn strict, right?

Sean Allen: And it was so frustrating. And and I could get C programs to compile. It didn't really dawn on me the fact that my C programs were segfaulting all the time and didn't really run for very long, but it was like, thank you for the cookie that it compiled, you know. Now I can move on to the other thing, but I spent years developing an intuition of how I could do stuff in C so that my programs didn't die and collapse. And And now all I want is I like I recognize like I had all these rules for myself for writing concurrent C and C++ and to keep myself from segfaulting programs. And even even though I became really rigorous with that, I'm a human and I screw stuff up all the time, and I would much rather have a compiler to help me with that. And so there's a lot of stuff in like OCaml and other languages like it, uh, F Sharp.

F# and.NET

Host: Can can can can we talk can we talk a little bit about F Sharp?

Sean Allen: Yes.

Host: For folks who have not used F Sharp, but they might have used C Sharp or TypeScript, how would you describe F Sharp and why it's different? And it right it's it's a language that Microsoft created or or they champion. I'm not sure if they created it.

Sean Allen: It so it came out of Microsoft Research. Um, the there's a fellow Don Syme who is really responsible for everything F Sharp. And it basically started as, uh, OCaml for.NET, where.NET at the time was just C Sharp and the.NET runtime.

Host: And and.NET is Microsoft's framework where it was really easy to access. I remember Windows APIs, had a lot of utility functions. It was their everything framework.

Sean Allen: Yeah it basically their version of the JVM.

Host: Yeah.

Sean Allen: Right. Um, and I have no special insight into it, but from somebody who was around when all those things happened, there was a whole bunch of legal kerfuffle with Microsoft adding Windows-specific APIs to their version of Java, and Sun threatening to sue them or something.

Host: and so I think Anders Hejlsberg on this podcast uh, shared the detail that they needed to develop C Sharp and I guess.NET as well because of a pending or or active Sun lawsuit. And so they could no longer use Java even though they wanted to use it, and that kind of settled it. So they built.NET.

Sean Allen: It did. And And.NET was was great because they took like pretty much everything they learned from the JVM and things where ideas have been baked into the JVM that would be kind of hard to change at that point, and they did different things which at the time seemed like much better ideas. People argue about whether they are or not at this point, but it doesn't really matter. But you know,.NET is a very nice platform, um, etc. for everything and they had one language basically that was on it which was C Sharp, which is an awful lot like Java. It has differences, but fundamentally the basic semantics of the language are the same.

Host: Very similar.

Sean Allen: Yeah. Um and so F# was a hey, let's bring some different semantics, let's bring some different stuff to this, which was originally like let's try to bring OCaml. And I think the thing that's amazing about F# is is not really specifically any language features from it um because it it has an awful lot of the things that OCaml has, but then it doesn't have some. And some people really like to complain about the stuff that it doesn't have who are big OCaml fans or whatever. But the thing that F# brought in a way that I've never really seen for anything else is it is it fits so well onto.NET as a platform and it fits so well. It's really the most seamless experience I've ever seen for something like I I did a lot of stuff with Scala and other languages on the JVM and there are lots of rough edges with with interacting with um Java where F# doesn't have that.

And F# developed in a lot of ways a lot more slowly and you can see how Don did this beautiful job of not running ahead with F# and and making a language which would be hard on the integration and having lots of rough edges and there would be like we're going to push this a little bit forward and we're going to wait for the.NET runtime to catch up to us so that everything continues to work and oh now the.NET runtime has added some stuff and it's you can see this thing where it's like ah F# pushes forward a little and then oh clearly this inspired like the.NET team some and there's like a symbiotic relationship was there. And over the years an awful lot of the really interesting and cool features from F# have made their way into uh C# and about the only thing that's really missing at a semantic level is actually the uh the sum types with exhaustive matching.

And based on the changes that have happened in the few years with C# it really looks like eventually even that would probably be incorporated into C#.

Pony and safe concurrency

Host: And another language I wanted to ask you about is Pony.

Sean Allen: Yes.

Host: What is Pony?

Sean Allen: Pony is a uh is an open source language that I work on. It was originally created by uh a friend of mine who uh uh we both went to a uh a college for people who had not done particularly well in high school

Host: Yep.

Sean Allen: and were in danger of say failing out and being high school dropouts where it was a it was an early college that would take people in like that who were not good in high school of which both my friend Sylvan and I were like that and Sylvan was actually the one who was like hey if you learn Perl you can come to Boston we can work on all this stuff together. Yeah. So I had gone off to work at a a place that was we were trying to build a high speed data processing stuff for banks and we started off by doing that for doing consulting with one of the big banks in New York City and we were just doing different consulting jobs and we were looking at stuff and around the time we were doing that I was thinking about what a system like this would look like and how I'd want to build it etc and everything and big part of it was it was like it needs to be really fast, right?

So this rules out a whole class of languages and it needed to be fast and have latency guarantees in a way that the JVM itself made really difficult and was for and for inside of banks was reserved for specialized things of either using C++ or the Azul

Host: When when you're saying the JVM made it difficult was it because of garbage collection was because of

Sean Allen: garbage collection latency issues etc. There's been a lot of work on the JVM since then.

Host: of garbage collection it's like sometimes your latency will spike like a normal function that should I don't know take this many milliseconds it could take way longer because garbage collection just kicked off not randomly.

Sean Allen: Particularly at that time on the standard of uh available to everyone uh JVM versions all the garbage collection was stopped the world which literally means in order to collect garbage everything has to stop and so you have a request that's just come in and your latency is going to go from yeah milliseconds to huge spikes this would be very bad in like trading systems etc so like the JVM was used primarily for systems that ran alongside trading systems which were you know where but even then it could still cause problems you have you have a risk system which is supposed to be evaluating uh whether you should shut down trading on particular things or not um and it has a spike like that that can still be hugely expensive and whatnot so there was a company uh they made a uh they still do um uh Azul systems they and they made a JVM which was pauseless um but it cost a lot of money so most projects didn't actually use it etc and whatnot and so we were we were looking at okay we're trying to replace the JVM type systems for stuff where people don't want to pay for Azul and we need something which will be really fast and we also need something where the the guarantee that we had to make for people was we're not going to lose any of your data and we're not going to mess any of it up which is concurrency and for speed close to the metal for whatever that means in terms of having some level of control over data locality etc and all of the things that go into being fast um if folks are interested in it looking looking into uh mechanical sympathy a lot of the stuff that Martin Thompson has done there um could be really interesting but we were looking for this collection of characteristics where we need to know it's working and we in in like our guarantees around not messing up your data were incredibly important to us and I was like I know C I'm good at C um I write C++ like it's still 1998 so I don't know if I would call myself good at C++ I still write C++ like it's 1998 for the most part and I was like, I don't think that we can meet all of these guarantees and I certainly don't think that I can hire people to work on a startup salary who would be able to pull this off with something like that.

And I was like, I don't know what we're going to do for this, but we continue to do consulting in this. And for one of the few useful things that's ever happened to me with LinkedIn, um Sylvan, who I hadn't talked to in a few years, sent me a message and said, hey, look at this thing that I made. And it was a it was an early version of Pony where he'd been working at Morgan Stanley.

Host: Yep.

Sean Allen: And he had built a thing that looked like a it was it was basically C, right? Um and it was an actor model type thing, which we could go into the actor model in a bit. But uh it was all written in people had to write stuff in C

Host: Yep.

Sean Allen: on top of it. And it came with all of the problems that C still had in terms of concurrency and seg faulting and everything that it had way back when I picked it instead of Ada. And the runtime worked really well, but the people who were writing the C on top of it had to be really expert and had to do things just right or they would mess up all of the great things that the runtime could give them. And so Sylvan decided, I'm going to go off. I'm going to learn a whole bunch of math so I can get really good at type system stuff. And I'm going to go off and I'm going to make my own programming language and he did a PhD at Imperial in the UK to do all of that. And the thing that popped out of the end of that was Pony. And he sent me the thing of, hey, look what I made. And it was Pony. And I looked at it for what we were trying to do at Wallaroo and I was like, this is actually kind of great for us.

Host: was a startup where he worked at an AI company, right?

Sean Allen: Yeah. Wallaroo eventually became an AI company. At at that point in time, it was a we're trying to sell high-speed data processing to banks, etc. and whatnot. Pony, nobody nobody had used it at all whatsoever. Um there were like the best that we could say when we decided to adopt it and people would be like what's that? We'd be like oh well it started as an idea at Morgan Stanley which can actually buy you an awful lot of awful lot of room when you're trying to sell the banks and the fact that Jane Street was basically the primary user of of OCaml anywhere in the world and OCaml had become completely associated with Jane Street at that point. People are like oh so you gonna you gonna be like the pony what Jane Street is to OCaml and we're like well if we're successful enough yes that that's kind of the idea.

So that's a lot of backstory to to answer the question. Pony is a a language which is absolutely in some way descended from the ML family of stuff. It has some it has a lot of stuff in common with OCaml. Um it has some stuff in common with F Sharp. Um it has some stuff in common with Rust because of that um where it's very much aimed at making it easy to write fast concurrent programs which are highly asynchronous and make it so that all of the rules that I learned uh to keep stuff from seg faulting are things that the compiler will enforce for you instead of well instead of instead of you doing which what I what I would do which is an invariably screw something up.

Host: Yeah.

Sean Allen: Um and and have it crash on you.

Host: Yeah I think you described pony makes illegal states unrepresentable.

Sean Allen: A large majority of them yes which and in that way it has a lot in common with Rust like one of the but the the model for how it does that in terms of concurrency is very different. I find the actor model which where um which is probably at this point most popular from Elixir and maybe that used to be you could say that it was it was Erlang but now it's probably really Elixir on that that the actor model makes it uh much easier to reason about concurrency and um pony you a built-in concurrency model the same way that Elixir and Erlang do in a way that you don't get with uh something like Rust. And is very much the type system and everything is very much built around making it really easy to do asynchronous programming. Um, and I think it has just one of the best experiences for doing that combination of things where there are other languages like Rust which are very good at providing you with um uh guarantees and whatnot, but aren't necessarily this full kind of uh uh omakase um sort of thing for no, actually here's how you do fearless concurrency.

You're you're not picking and choosing a bunch of things. We've picked a bunch of things and we put them together for for you.

Rethinking garbage collection

Host: And can we talk a little bit about garbage collection? And we just mentioned how it's slow, but I'll quote you in uh a blog post you previously wrote or this I think this was a talk. It says most engineers think garbage collection is slow. They're not wrong about their experience. Stop the world collectors really do destroy all your tail latencies. But garbage collection is slow confuses the symptom with the cause. What is the cause? And I mean the symptom is that sometimes the world stops, right?

Sean Allen: So, well the first thing I would say is that most people when they think of garbage collection, they think of like what the JVM does. Um, I think of garbage collection as a different thing, which is that garbage collection is a mechanism by which your program frees memory that it no longer needs. Because um there is there is definitely this thing where sometimes people think about you on one side you're doing like malloc and free and whatnot and on the other side you have garbage collection. But if you want to go fast, you you don't malloc and free all the time because this is really slow. These are system calls. The first step that people do is they they allocate a whole bunch of memory at once and then they start like slicing off little bits to themselves using like there are things called like slab allocators.

They might do arena allocation. There's a whole whole set of memory allocators. And then it becomes, well, I am now managing this memory. How do I know when it's free and when I can use, when I can, when I can free it, etc. and what not? You're already halfway to what most people think of as garbage collection at that point. And it becomes, it becomes a, a story of how am I doing these things and what is the, what are the tradeoffs that these things come with? And in terms of the JVM, uh, all of the memory is basically reachable from anywhere from any thread in the, and so it's very hard to be able to free memory in a way that doesn't cause you to have to do a stop the world. And the stuff [clears throat] that concurrent collectors like, uh, Java has the Shenandoah collector, Azul has theirs do, is actually really impressive engineering for how they manage to do what's called concurrent garbage collection.

Pony has a garbage collector, which is, instead of having a stop the world, what you have instead is that, this is, this is a bit of a lie in order to get to the truth, uh, without going too deep, but each actor has its own heap is the way that somebody could think about it, which is also how people describe stuff for the Erlang VM BEAM, which is also not technically true there, but it makes it easier to think about. And that each actor is responsible for freeing memory that it's used. So you do not, you do not garbage collect and stop the entire thing. What you do is instead, is that when an actor is done doing some work, it can check to see through some heuristic, do I have memory that I can, that I can free?

Host: an actor we can think of like as a, something like a thread, maybe a bit more lightweight than that, but it's kind of your own kind of like world that's kind of separate from other actors or.

Sean Allen: Yep. And so instead of, instead of I'm going to stop my entire program in order to free memory, it's like, oh hey, well, I did 10 application operations and now I'm going to do one memory freeing operation. And what you, what you end up with with with like pony and with other concurrent memory freeing things that are like that where the things can operate independent of one another is you end up with these things where instead of having these really spiky latency things like people are used to seeing if they run things like Cassandra or whatnot on a standard JVM setup where it's just like my tail latencies are really bad is that you just get basically flat latencies for the most part or or a tiny little bridge. And the thing that you give up on that is that at your fastest moment you have a little bit less throughput than you might otherwise.

And this is still a garbage collection, but it's just it's it's an entirely different like take on garbage collection and and it's it's a really the difference between that and what a lot of people end up doing in sophisticated, you know, memory allocators that they write for themselves and whatnot is that at this point they've completely basically taken themselves as a programmer out of the equation. They've come up with an algorithm or something for deciding when memory should be freed instead of them having to try and code in what the particular rules for it would be.

Software correctness

Host: So let's talk about software correctness. How do you define software correctness?

Sean Allen: I would define software correctness as my program does what I expected it to do at at a at a really loose level. I tend to talk about things in terms of invariance, right, which is a more formal specification term. But in in the end invariant or it's it's a guarantee of which even more loosely is my my software is doing what I expected it to do. But in a lot of cases people don't necessarily know what they expect their software to do. They know when it 's not working, but they don't necessarily know when it's working. But software correctness is really about like it is a way of approaching software and a way of thinking about it of being of of knowing that it is it is upholding what it is supposed to do. It is software which is you know which is going to do its business purpose or whatever it was written for and it's not going to wake anybody up at 2:00 in the morning.

That that is correct software.

Testing as a means to an end

Host: correct software clearly you want to know do some testing but you wrote a very interesting blog post which I'm going to quote you. No one cares about testing. summary: 在与 Gergely Orosz 的对谈中，Antithesis 红队工程师兼 Pony 语言维护者 Sean Allen 深入探讨了如何在全栈层面实现软件正确性。结合他在 Ada、OCaml、F#、Pony、Wallaroo 以及微软研究院机密计算团队的实战经验，Allen 指出团队应当将保障前置到 ML 风格的类型系统、Actor 隔离以及前期设计对齐中，而不应把代码审查或 CI/CD 当作质量门禁。他进一步解析了单 Actor 独立垃圾回收如何以少量峰值吞吐量为代价换取平稳的尾延迟，为何像银行测试这样的有状态测试工作负载能比单纯随机检查更深入地暴露分布式缺陷，FFI 边界与推测执行侧信道如何削弱供应链安全与机密计算保障，以及为何保持软件的可塑性并在前期放慢节奏能避免技术债演变为沉重负担。

mainPoints.point: 将正确性前置到类型系统与系统设计中
mainPoints.explanation: Allen 认为团队不应将代码审查或 CI/CD 视为事后捕获缺陷的质量门禁，而应通过 ML 风格的类型系统或 Actor 隔离来编码合法状态与状态转换，从根源上使整类内存和并发错误无法被表达。

mainPoints.point: 设计有状态的测试工作负载，而非盲目随机测试
mainPoints.explanation: 基于示例的单元测试容易留下可被绕过的盲区，而均匀分布的随机操作只会在浅层状态间进行漫无目的的游走。面向分布式系统的有效基于属性测试，需要将银行测试等清晰的不变量与故障注入相结合，并用工作负载驱动深层状态转换。

mainPoints.point: Actor 局部垃圾回收可有效拉平尾延迟
mainPoints.explanation: 当任意线程都能访问任意内存时，全局停顿式的 JVM 垃圾回收器会引发剧烈的延迟抖动。通过隔离每个 Actor 的堆内存并由其独立释放，Pony 和 Erlang 等语言以适度降低峰值吞吐量为代价，换取了可预测且平稳的尾延迟。

mainPoints.point: 现有运行时在供应链与硬件层面仍存在安全缺口
mainPoints.explanation: 冷却期和仓库分叉等防御手段十分脆弱，因为主流语言默认赋予第三方依赖完整的进程权限，即便是对象能力模型也会被 FFI 调用绕过。同时，推测执行会通过侧信道攻击泄露机密信息，这一点连机密计算至今仍无法彻底消除。

mainPoints.point: 通过保持软件可塑性与前期对齐来管控技术债
mainPoints.explanation: 技术债只有在团队必须偿还时才会造成伤害，因此早期系统应当保持可塑性和易于替换，避免过早追求完美。在项目初期放慢节奏，就术语、规格说明和可观测性达成对齐，能够避免数周的无效返工，并在后续实现持久的开发提速。
